summary: A feature piece about outdoor yoga and fitness in Central Park during autumn 2023. It follows participants such as Jasmine Martin, Olivia Thompson and Steve Richardson, and instructors Akash Gupta, Jenny Park and Master Lin, describing how classes from yoga to bootcamp to tai chi connect people with nature and build community. It closes with journalist Ellie Saunders reflecting on the cultural shift toward communal outdoor wellness.
one_line: Central Park's outdoor yoga and fitness classes in autumn 2023 foster connection with nature, community and a cultural shift in urban wellness.
key_facts: Jasmine Martin, a yoga enthusiast, attends a Tuesday morning outdoor yoga class in Central Park; the scene opens on September 5th, 2023.
Jasmine Martin moved to open-air classes after years of indoor practice, calling it "a transformative experience."
Akash Gupta instructs the outdoor yoga sessions and has guided them since September 10th, five days after Jasmine's first park yoga session.
The yoga group is diverse in ages, abilities and backgrounds, reflecting the inclusive spirit of the sessions.
Olivia Thompson, a recent convert to outdoor fitness, says it is about "connecting with your environment" and being part of something bigger than yourself.

Jenny Park, a celebrity fitness trainer previously known for boutique studios, runs a weekend fitness bootcamp in the park using benches for dips, pathways for sprints and open fields for bodyweight exercises.
Steve Richardson, a regular at Jenny Park's bootcamp, says uneven ground or gentle slopes demand greater stability and core strength.
Master Lin leads tai chi enthusiasts in the evening, after midday Pilates classes and afternoon dance-fitness sessions.
Park participants include corporate executives in sportswear, parents in post-pram jogging groups and artists.
By mid-September the park's autumn colors formed a backdrop for fitness activities.
Ellie Saunders, a local journalist covering urban trends, says moving a workout outdoors can reshape people's routines and relationships with their environment.
By October, groups exercising together had replaced solitary joggers, a change the article calls a cultural shift.
